mcqs.question: What should you determine before proposing a fix for a shard receiving disproportionate traffic?
options: Whether it's a hot key on one shard, a badly distributed shard, or evenly spread load on too few shards
Which cloud region the shard's physical hardware is located in
Whether the shard's database engine version is the newest one available
How many total shards existed when the system originally launched
mcqs.explanation: The three-way diagnosis — hot key, bad distribution, or under-provisioning — determines which fix actually helps; each of the other fixes wastes effort on the wrong cause. Hardware region, engine version, and launch-time shard count don't distinguish between these causes.

mcqs.question: In the worked example, per-shard QPS shows shard-03 far above the others. What additional check confirms whether this is a hot key or a hot shard?
options: Checking the shard's disk temperature and physical hardware age
Comparing shard-03's QPS against the theoretical maximum QPS of its hardware
Restarting the shard's database process and observing whether QPS changes afterward
Breaking down shard-03's traffic by individual key to see if one key accounts for most of it
mcqs.explanation: A key-level breakdown on the hot shard reveals whether one key dominates its traffic (a hot key) or the load is spread evenly across many keys (a hot shard from bad distribution). Hardware theoretical maximums, disk temperature, or a restart don't reveal which of those two causes is at play.

mcqs.question: What ongoing cost does virtual (consistent) hashing add in exchange for cheap rebalancing?
options: It permanently increases the storage size of every row by a fixed amount
It requires every physical shard to be identically sized forever
It adds one extra lookup hop — key to virtual shard to physical node — on every request, indefinitely
It removes the ability to add new physical shards to the cluster in the future
mcqs.explanation: Every request now resolves through an extra indirection layer, which is a permanent per-request cost, not a one-time migration cost. It doesn't inflate row size, doesn't require uniform shard sizes, and doesn't block adding more physical shards — quite the opposite, it's what makes adding them cheap.

mcqs.question: Why does resharding the entire dataset typically fail to fix a hot-key problem?
options: Resharding always takes longer than isolating a single key, regardless of the cause
The hot key's traffic follows it to whichever shard it lands on under the new layout, so the imbalance persists
Resharding tools are incompatible with datasets that contain any hot keys at all
Resharding requires downtime, while isolating a key does not, making it strictly worse in every case
mcqs.explanation: The imbalance is caused by one key's traffic volume, not by the shard layout, so a new layout just relocates the same hot key to a (possibly different) hot shard. It isn't a downtime or tooling-compatibility issue — it's that resharding doesn't address the actual cause.
